Lunar Landing Site Navigator

Compare landing sites and dates near the Moon's south pole: where the Sun and Earth sit against the skyline, how long they stay up, and what that means for power and direct communication with Earth. Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons. Terrain comes from the LOLA elevation map. Select a point on the map or pick a site, then press Play to watch the light move.

South pole, lit as it will be

Built from the LOLA elevation map at about 630 m per pixel and the Sun's position from JPL Horizons. Select any point to analyse it as a landing site. The map is a visual guide; the numbers below come from the site's own skyline, which is more precise.

What happens if you land here

Why the south pole is different

  • The Moon barely tilts, about 1.5°. At the pole the Sun never climbs: it circles the horizon once every 29.5 days.
  • Because the Sun is so low, a ridge a few hundred metres high can hide it for days, and a crater floor can stay dark for billions of years. Press Play on the map to watch the shadows swing round.
  • Earth does not rise and set the way the Sun does. It hovers in one part of the sky and bobs up and down about every 27 days, so a lander loses its direct radio link whenever Earth dips behind the skyline.
  • Try this: compare the ridge next to Shackleton crater with the crater floor, 13 km away. Then compare both with Apollo 11 near the equator.

Same sunlight, three ways to mount a solar panel

Full-sun hours count how long the panel would need to face the Sun head-on to collect the same light. A flat panel wastes low sunlight; an upright one catches it.

A body counts as visible when its centre is above the skyline. Earth must also clear the minimum margin. This is geometric visibility: it does not model antennas, ground stations or battery size. Full-sun hours measure head-on sunlight time for the chosen panel, not energy.

Hard constraints

Select a cell or a row to load it into the views above. Slip tolerance counts the passing landing dates on each side on this date grid; times between grid dates are not tested. "At least" means the run reached the end of the grid. The star marks candidates that no other passing candidate beats on every measure in the table, counting early and late slip as separate measures.

Sun and Earth positions: NASA JPL Horizons. Terrain: NASA LRO Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA). Visibility is geometric and uses the centre of each disk. Code written with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic).
